description: We’re a team of Computer Technology Engineering students from UDEM (Universidad de Monterrey) in Monterrey. We’re interested in the Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts challenge. We like the idea of building something that helps astronauts understand what’s happening to their own bodies on long missions, especially when they’re too far from Earth to rely on a doctor.
summary: On Mars, a message to a doctor on Earth can take up to 22 minutes to arrive. On long missions, astronauts must notice changes in their own bodies first. HUMAN ROVER is an educational simulation with game elements that teaches astronauts to monitor and act on their health during a 36-month mission to Mars. Guided by Laika, explorers log monthly health indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood and vision), and each one turns green, yellow or red against their own Earth baseline. Its core is a clickable 3D human body that lights up where spaceflight affects it at each stage of the trip. Tapping a body part starts a guided self-check that explains what may be happening, what to do, and when to alert the crew or flight surgeons, always citing NASA sources. XP, streaks and mission patches keep the routine going. HUMAN ROVER turns NASA Human Research Program knowledge into a tool astronauts can understand, practice with and act on when help is far away.
details:
HUMAN ROVER is a web app that simulates a 36-month crewed mission to Mars in four stages: the trip there (months 1–8), life on Mars (9–27), the trip home (28–35) and back on Earth (36). Moving the mission month changes the environment, the music, the daily tasks and the health risks, because NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight (radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields and a hostile closed environment) affect the body differently at each stage.

How it works

  • Create your explorer and Earth baseline. Each astronaut chooses a male or female body and starts from Earth values. All results compare against their own baseline, not a generic "normal".
  • Mission Control. A month slider, the most urgent alert, a "Today" task list (check-in, exercise, diary or report to Earth) and Laika's guidance for the current stage.
  • Monthly check-in. Heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep hours, mood and vision. Each value turns green, yellow or red instantly, with a "how?" line (how to measure it) and a "why?" line linking the NASA risk behind it.
  • Check yourself (guided self-check). Tap a body part on the 3D model, pick a symptom and answer a few questions. The app ranks the most likely causes for the current mission month, then walks a decision tree to a result: what may be happening, what to do, and when to alert the crew medical officer or flight surgeons. Red-flag symptoms (chest pain, fainting, shortness of breath, sudden vision change) skip the questions and go straight to an emergency alert.
  • Learn. Lessons from NASA risk pages, filtered by hazard, body part and month, each with a short quiz and its source.
  • Trends. Dynamic charts of sleep, resting heart rate and mood across the 36 months, with the Earth baseline and the months on Mars marked.
  • Diary and reports. A mission diary searchable by month and a queue of reports to Earth, sent oldest first, as with real communication delays.
  • Gamification. XP, check-in streaks, mission patches, an exercise log based on the ISS treadmill, bike and resistance device, and a "Mission complete" screen with your results.

Tech stack

  • React 18 + Vite 5 (front end), deployed on Netlify
  • Three.js through React Three Fiber and drei for the interactive 3D body
  • Blender to cut the CC0 body models into clickable parts
  • Figma for wireframes and screen design
  • Our own JavaScript data structures (no libraries): decision tree, max-heap, queue, stack and sorted array with binary search
  • Node.js built-in test runner: 28 automated tests, including edge cases
  • All content stored as JSON data with its NASA source, so new symptoms or lessons are added as data, not code
  • Progress saved in the browser (localStorage): health data never leaves the user's device

Innovation highlights

  • A body that changes with the mission. The 3D model lights up where each hazard affects the body in that month, so astronauts see how spaceflight changes them over time.
  • Context-aware self-check. The same symptom gives a different likely cause in month 1 than in month 30, because a max-heap ranks causes by how much each NASA risk matters at that stage.
  • Personal baseline. Every color compares the astronaut against their own Earth values.
  • Data trust. Every lesson and result links to its NASA or CSA source, and the app separates what was learned on the ISS from what NASA expects on Mars.
  • Built for distance. Works in the browser without a server, with reports queued for Earth and clear rules for when to call for help.

Assumptions and limits

  • HUMAN ROVER is an educational tool, not a medical device. The green, yellow and red limits are demonstration values; in a real mission flight surgeons would set them for each astronaut.
  • No human has lived on Mars yet, so Mars content is based on what NASA expects from ISS research.
  • Values are entered by the astronaut today. Next steps: real sensors, validation with flight surgeons, user testing and a VR version.
